title: Toward the Goldilocks Blind Compression of Quantum States
claim: A compression model squeezes the input through a narrow bottleneck then reconstructs it, using a small set of concrete modules.
layout: Top funnel diagram above aligned circuit; left-to-right, dashed vertical guides
description: The figure has two aligned layers. On top is a bowtie-shaped schematic. A blue trapezoid labeled Encoder narrows from n to k at a central Bottleneck. An orange trapezoid labeled Decoder widens back out to n. Below it is a quantum circuit with three horizontal wires, from top to bottom: |0>, |0> and |psi>. Registers on the wires are labeled A through G. A blue gradient box U is the encoder unitary. An orange gradient box V is the decoder unitary. The latent output of U is labeled rho_enc, and a curved wire carries it into V. Dashed vertical lines tie the schematic to the circuit positions. A dashed arrow loops along the bottom from the input |psi> to the output rho_rec. The caption reads 'Goal: <psi|rho_rec|psi> ≈ 1'. Blue and orange mark encoder and decoder throughout.
caption: General structure of a QAE that compresses an n-qubit input state |ψ⟩into a k-qubit latent system and subsequently reconstructs the state using a decoder. Labels A–G identify the individual quantum registers.
abstract: Quantum autoencoders (QAEs) are learning architectures that compress quantum data into a low-dimensional latent state while preserving the information needed for reconstruction. We study blind single-copy compression of quantum states through a $k$-qubit bottleneck and investigate the minimal circuit width required to attain the information-theoretic optimum under average infidelity. Between the conventional architecture, which is narrow but nonuniversal, and fully general \emph{completely positive and trace preserving} (CPTP) realizations, which are universal but overparameterized, we identify a balanced regime. We prove that for every distribution of pure $n$-qubit states, there exists a QAE with $k$ encoder ancillas and $n$ decoder ancillas that achieves the optimal fidelity over all CPTP encoder--decoder pairs. The encoder-side statement is sharp in that we construct source families for which every optimal scheme necessarily uses at least $k$ encoder ancillas, thereby determining the universal encoder threshold exactly. On the decoder side, we show that isometric decoders are optimal for several analytically tractable source families, but we also exhibit an explicit counterexample demonstrating that decoder isometry is not universally sufficient. Nevertheless, numerical experiments indicate that the performance gap is practically negligible.
